title: Pure Spectrum and Dispersive Power
notes: A prism forms a spectrum because refractive index varies with wavelength. In normal dispersion, violet has a larger index and deviation than red. A pure spectrum has narrow, well-separated colour images with little overlap.
For a thin prism, angular dispersion is Δδ=(nv−nr)A and yellow mean deviation is δy=(ny−1)A. Their ratio is ω=Δδ/δy=(nv−nr)/(ny−1).
Worked example: if δy=3° and ω=0.06, the red–violet spread is Δδ=0.18°. A material with twice the dispersive power gives twice the spread at the same mean deviation.
To obtain a purer spectrum, use a narrow slit, collimate the incident beam and focus the dispersed rays with a lens. A wide slit broadens each colour image and causes neighbouring bands to overlap.
A spectrometer uses a collimator slit and telescope to form and inspect a sharp spectrum. Resolution improves when the source image is narrow and the optical alignment is correct.

A pure spectrum is formed when each colour is brought to its own sharp image and those images do not overlap. A slit at the focus of a collimating lens sends parallel light into the prism, and a telescope then focuses each colour separately.

specificConditions: **Dispersion Definition:** Dispersion is the separation of white light into its constituent colors (spectrum) due to the dependence of the refractive index $n$ on the wavelength $\lambda$ of light ($n(\lambda)$).

**Cauchy's Equation:** For many transparent materials, the refractive index follows Cauchy's equation $n(\lambda) = A + B/\lambda^2 + C/\lambda^4$. This explains why blue light ($\lambda$ smaller) is refracted more than red light ($\lambda$ larger).

**Prism Validity:** The formula for dispersive power $\omega = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1)$ assumes small angle of deviation and that the prism is in air. For non-thin prisms or different mediums, angular dispersion depends on the geometry.
